summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity, the shifted values \(Y_k=a_{3773+k}+1\) satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence; a modular Fibonacci-matrix computation with \(p=195318521017\) and \(j=249580073232\) gives \(Y_j\equiv0\) and \(Y_{j+1}\equiv1\pmod p\). Hence \(a_{3774+j}\) and \(a_{3775+j}\) are both divisible by \(p\), so their gcd is at least \(2\), making the actual next term strictly smaller than one plus their sum and contradicting the claimed identity at \(n=3776+j\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\qquad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We disprove the conjecture. In fact, it is enough to disprove its first assertion
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\qquad(n\geq3775),                 \tag{1}
\]
since the full conjecture asserts this formula together with two other formulas.

The argument is by contradiction. Assume that (1) holds for every \(n\geq3775\). We will propagate this assumed linear recurrence to a very distant index, where a modular computation shows that two consecutive terms have a large common divisor. The defining gcd recurrence at the next index will then be incompatible with (1).

Define a Fibonacci-type sequence \(Y_k\) by
\[
Y_0=a_{3773}+1,\qquad Y_1=a_{3774}+1,
\qquad Y_{k+2}=Y_{k+1}+Y_k\quad(k\geq0).                 \tag{2}
\]
Every \(Y_k\) is positive. Indeed, the first two terms are positive, and positivity is preserved by (2).

Under assumption (1), for every \(m\geq3773\) we have
\[
a_m=Y_{m-3773}-1.                                      \tag{3}
\]
For \(m=3773,3774\), this is exactly the definition of \(Y_0,Y_1\). For \(m\geq3775\), suppose it is known at the two preceding indices. Then (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_m
 &=1+a_{m-1}+a_{m-2}\\
 &=1+(Y_{m-3774}-1)+(Y_{m-3775}-1)\\
 &=Y_{m-3774}+Y_{m-3775}-1\\
 &=Y_{m-3773}-1,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality is (2). Thus induction proves (3).

We now give the finite and modular computations used in the argument. Set
\[
p=195318521017,
\qquad j=249580073232.
\]
Only the fact \(p\geq2\) will be needed; primality is not required.

Direct iteration of the original gcd recurrence from \(a_1=a_2=1\) through indices 3773 and 3774 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3773}={}&,\\[2mm]
a_{3774}={}&.
\end{aligned}
\]
At each iteration this computation takes the gcd of the preceding two displayed integers and applies the defining formula, so it is a finite computation entirely in the integers. Reducing the two resulting values plus 1 modulo \(p\) gives
\[
Y_0\equiv77940394259\pmod p,
\qquad
Y_1\equiv99768150822\pmod p.                            \tag{4}
\]

To advance the recurrence (2) efficiently modulo \(p\), let
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equation (2) implies, by induction on \(k\),
\[
\binom{Y_{k+1}}{Y_k}
\equiv
T^k\binom{Y_1}{Y_0}\pmod p.                            \tag{5}
\]
A repeated-squaring computation modulo \(p\) gives
\[
T^j\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
21827756563&117378126758\\
117378126758&99768150822
\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p.                                                \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, this calculation uses only the identity
\(T^{r+s}=T^rT^s\) and reduction of all four entries modulo \(p\). One convenient addition chain for the exponent is
\[
\begin{gathered}
1,2,3,6,7,14,28,29,58,116,232,464,928,929,1858,1859,
3718,3719,7438,14876,29752,59504,119008,119009,\\
238018,476036,952072,1904144,3808288,3808289,7616578,
7616579,15233158,30466316,30466317,60932634,60932635,\\
121865270,243730540,487461080,974922160,974922161,
1949844322,3899688644,7799377288,15598754576,\\
15598754577,31197509154,62395018308,124790036616,
249580073232.
\end{gathered}
\]
Each even entry is obtained by doubling the indicated preceding exponent, while the entries immediately following an even entry by 1 are obtained by multiplying once more by \(T\). Successive modular matrix multiplication along this chain yields (6).

Combining (4), (5), and (6), the final matrix-vector multiplication is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
21827756563&117378126758\\
117378126758&99768150822
\end{pmatrix}
\binom{99768150822}{77940394259}
\equiv
\binom{1}{0}\pmod{195318521017}.
\]
Thus
\[
Y_{j+1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
Y_j\equiv0\pmod p.                                    \tag{7}
\]
This is the essential modular obstruction.

Put
\[
N=3774+j=249580077006,
\qquad
B=a_N,
\qquad
A=a_{N+1}.
\]
Since \(N\geq3775\), formula (3) applies. The index calculations are
\[
N-3773=j+1,
\qquad
(N+1)-3773=j+2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
B=Y_{j+1}-1,
\qquad
A=Y_{j+2}-1.                                           \tag{8}
\]
The first congruence in (7) and the first equality in (8) show that
\[
p\mid B.                                               \tag{9}
\]
Moreover, by (2),
\[
A=Y_{j+2}-1=Y_{j+1}+Y_j-1=(Y_{j+1}-1)+Y_j.
\]
Both summands on the right are divisible by \(p\), by (7), so
\[
p\mid A.                                               \tag{10}
\]

We also need that \(A\) and \(B\) are positive. Since \(Y_j\) is positive and divisible by \(p\), (7) implies \(Y_j\geq p\). Also, using (2),
\[
Y_{j+1}=Y_j+Y_{j-1}\geq p+1,
\]
because \(j\geq1\) and every \(Y_k\geq1\). Hence
\(B=Y_{j+1}-1\geq p>0\). Similarly,
\[
A=Y_{j+1}+Y_j-1>0.
\]

Let
\[
g=\gcd(A,B).
\]
By (9) and (10), \(p\mid g\). Since \(g>0\), this implies
\[
g\geq p\geq2.                                         \tag{11}
\]

We record the elementary inequality that now creates the contradiction. If positive integers \(A,B\) have gcd \(g\geq2\), then
\[
g+\frac{A+B}{g}<1+A+B.                                \tag{12}
\]
To prove it, write \(A=ga\) and \(B=gb\), where \(a,b\geq1\). Then
\[
g+\frac{A+B}{g}=g+a+b.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
1+A+B=1+ga+gb.
\]
Their difference is
\[
(1+ga+gb)-(g+a+b)
 =1+(g-1)(a+b)-g.
\]
Since \(a+b\geq2\), this is at least
\[
1+2(g-1)-g=g-1>0.
\]
This proves (12).

Now evaluate the original sequence at index
\[
N+2=249580077008.
\]
Its two preceding terms are \(A=a_{N+1}\) and \(B=a_N\), whose gcd is \(g\). Therefore the defining recurrence gives
\[
a_{N+2}=g+\frac{A+B}{g}.                               \tag{13}
\]
By (11) and (12),
\[
a_{N+2}<1+A+B.                                         \tag{14}
\]
But \(N+2\geq3775\), so the assumed conjectural formula (1) says
\[
a_{N+2}=1+a_{N+1}+a_N=1+A+B,                           \tag{15}
\]
contradicting (14).

Hence (1) cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). More explicitly, the argument gives the following finite dichotomy: either the claimed linear recurrence already fails at some index between 3775 and \(N+1=249580077007\), or, if it holds through that range, then the modular calculation forces a common divisor at least \(p\) for \(a_N,a_{N+1}\), and it fails at \(N+2=249580077008\). In either case there is an index \(n\geq3775\) for which the first asserted equality is false. Therefore the conjunction of all three claimed formulas, and thus the stated conjecture for A355898, is false.
